3.2 Synthesis of catalytic materials Catalytic materials play a critical role in reducing activation energy in reactions, thereby accelerating reaction rates and enhancing efficiency. They are extensively employed across various industries, including chemical, petroleum, environ- mental, pharmaceutical, and energy sectors.
83–85 While the synthesis of basic catalytic materials is relatively straightfor- ward, the development of high-performance catalysts presents significant challenges. This process requires precise control over the catalyst’s structure, along with careful regulation of its components and other influencing factors. Even when target- ing a single factor, the complexity remains considerable. For instance, the synthesis of multicomponent catalysts involves the adjustment of numerous components, creating a vast parameter space that traditional trial-and-error methods are ill-equipped to handle. 86 Furthermore, ensuring that the selected components offer the best performance remains a major challenge. 87,88 Therefore, there is an urgent need for new technologies capable of efficiently exploring large para- meter spaces to accelerate the synthesis of high-performance catalysts. SDLs present an effective and reliable solution for the synthesis of high-performance catalysts. 89,90 In this section, their application in synthesizing high-performance OER cata- lysts will be discussed. Luo et al. 90 have developed an artificial intelligence chemist platform for the automatic synthesis and intelligent optimiza- tion of oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalysts for Martian meteorites (Fig. 5(a)). The hardware part consists of a mobile robot and specialized chemical workstations dedicated to specific tasks, covering the entire process from chemical

Self-driving laboratory for mechanistic investigation In the fields of chemistry and materials science, mechanistic investigation is crucial for understanding the underlying pro- cesses of reactions. It provides a solid theoretical foundation for the development of new reactions, optimization of existing ones, and design of novel materials.
91,92 However, mechanistic investigation is inherently complex and challenging. 93,94 Tradi- tional research methods are limited in their ability to explore high-dimensional parameter spaces efficiently, making it diffi- cult to identify the optimal experimental conditions for mecha- nistic investigation. 95 Additionally, mechanistic insights are often hidden within the microscopic details of experimental data, and existing machine learning models lack the capability to automatically uncover these implicit correlations. 96,97 As a result, mechanistic investigation remains highly reliant on manual data analysis. In recent years, SDLs have been increas- ingly employed in chemistry and materials science research that requires exploration of high-dimensional parameter spaces. However, due to their stringent requirements for hard- ware precision and data processing capabilities, the application of SDLs in mechanistic research is still limited. In this section, the only publicly disclosed case of the SDL being used for molecular electrochemistry mechanistic investigation will be discussed. Liu et al. 98 reported a SDL that achieved an automated closed-loop study for the research on molecular electrochemi- cal mechanisms (Fig. 6(a)). The hardware part mainly consists of a flow chemistry module, an automatic electrochemical testing module, and a traditional single-cell electrochemical cell with a three-electrode configuration, as shown in Fig. 6(b). The software part includes a deep learning model for automatic cyclic voltammetry (CV) analysis and Bayesian optimization software. The deep learning model can provide the probability distribution of possible mechanisms based on CV data analy- sis, while the Bayesian optimization software quickly recom- mends experimental conditions with higher probabilities of a certain mechanism and feeds the results back to the hard- ware part for verification. 99,100 This platform autonomously

3.1 Forward design High-throughput screening (HTS) originated from the concept of ‘‘combinatorial synthesis and testing of entire multicomponent systems’’ proposed in the 1970s, and was first widely adopted in drug discovery. Over the past decade, HTS has gained momen- tum in materials science, enabling the parallel assessment of vast MOF libraries to identify candidates with promising properties. 45
Current HTS strategies for MOFs typically follow a funnel-like workflow (Fig. 4(a)). 91 First, structural datasets are collected and preprocessed (as discussed in the previous sec- tion), and then a series of compounds is generated based on the predefined spatial structures and connectivity rules of the frame- works. Second, the dataset is filtered using structural descriptors such as pore diameter, surface area, and desolvation stability. Third, these geometrical and physical descriptors are combined with simulated properties or first-principles calculations to establish structure–property relationships. Based on the observed trends, a small subset of top-performing and experimentally promising MOFs is selected for further in-depth study or synthesis. 92 Several previous review articles have provided comprehensive summaries of HTS strategies. 91,93,94 Traditionally, high-throughput screening processes for MOFs have relied on computationally intensive simulations such as DFT and GCMC. While these first-principles methods provide high accuracy, their scalability is limited by the sub- stantial time and computational resources required, especially when applied to large structural libraries. To overcome these limitations, recent advances in deep ML and AI have been increasingly integrated into HTS workflows. Heuristic optimi- zation methods, including GNNs, genetic algorithms, and more recently, generative diffusion models, have been employed to enhance or even replace traditional simulation approaches. These data-driven models enable rapid prediction of key prop- erties, such as gas adsorption capacity, thermal conductivity, and structural stability, based on learned patterns, significantly accelerating the screening process.
title: AI-driven advances in metal–organic frameworks: from data to design and applications

text: These models can rapidly screen a large number of chemical structures and prioritize promising candidates for experimental validation, thereby greatly streamlining MOF development in both time and resources. In particular, generative AI models based on deep learning architectures have shown the ability to propose novel, chemically valid frameworks tailored for specific applications. When coupled with simulation pipelines and property prediction tools, these models enable a closed-loop system that accelerates both discovery and optimization. This AI-driven paradigm not only enhances the efficiency and precision of material design but also sets the stage for autonomous laboratories and self-driving experi- mentation, opening new frontiers in materials science. In this review, we present an overview of recent advances at the intersection of AI and MOF research, with a focus on databases, algorithms, predictive modeling, synthesis and practical applica- tions (Fig. 1). Section 2 introduces the foundational components that underpin AI-driven MOF research, including curated data- bases, deep ML models and generative AI frameworks. Section 3 discusses AI-assisted material design and discovery workflows, highlighting forward design, inverse design, and active learning (AL) as key methodologies for navigating the vast MOF chemical space. Section 4 shifts the focus to AI-driven prediction and synthesis, where we detail recent progress in predicting intrinsic and functional properties, and guiding autonomous laboratory synthesis. Finally, Section 5 explores the application of AI- accelerated MOF development in diverse domains, including gas adsorption, separation, catalysis, water treatment, electronics, bio- medicine, and flame retardancy. By synthesizing insights across these topics, we aim to provide readers with a holistic under- standing of the opportunities, challenges, and emerging paradigms that AI brings to MOF research.

Complementing such data-driven catalyst design, further research has focused on identifying underlying electronic and structural descriptors to enhance prediction interpretability and transferability. Mou et al. combined DFT calculations and machine learning to identify key descriptors—including metal intrinsic properties, con- strained coordination geometries, and linker electronic effects—for predicting CO₂ reduction performance on UiO-66-supported single- atom catalysts. 183 The models accurately predicted limiting poten- tials for C₁ products and demonstrated strong transferability to new functionalized systems, providing an efficient strategy for screening high-performance electrocatalysts. In photocatalysis, Bhavya Jaksani et al. integrated Bayesian optimization into a continuous-flow system for MOF-derived CuO/TiO₂ photocatalysts. 184 The AI model dynamically tuned reaction parameters in real time, increasing CO₂ conversion yield and achieving a record-breaking methanol production rate of 2.3 mol g 1 h 1, which is 2 to 100 times higher than those reported for batch processes. This highlights how ML enhances both material performance and process control. While real-time optimization significantly advances reaction efficiency, understanding the key factors governing photocata- lytic performance remains essential for rational catalyst and process design. Gheytanzadeh et al. employed GPR with multi- ple kernels to model tetracycline photocatalytic degradation over MOFs, identifying illumination time and surface area as the most critical parameters influencing efficiency, consistent with photochemical mechanisms. 185 The GPR-Matern model demonstrated superior prediction accuracy (R² = 0.981), provid- ing a robust computational framework for optimizing antibio- tic wastewater treatment processes. In biocatalysis, Chai et al. pioneered the use of random forest models to predict enzyme loading, immobilization effi- ciency, and reusability in enzyme@MOF composites, achieving R² = 0.85 and prediction errors below 25%. 186 This not only reduced experimental cost but also clarified the influence of key features like pore size and enzyme molecular weight, advancing AI-assisted design of robust biocatalytic systems. These examples highlight how AI/ML connects atomic-scale structures with catalytic performance across scales. To over- come current challenges like dynamic active site changes and solvation effects, future research will benefit from integrating ML with in situ characterization and multi-scale simulation for autonomous catalyst design.

5.4 Catalysis AI and ML are transforming the development and refinement of MOF-based catalysts by facilitating data-driven innovations that surpass traditional empirical methods. Catalytic perfor- mance in MOFs depends heavily on active site structure (e.g., open metal centers, functionalized ligands, or embedded nano- particles), pore-mediated mass transport, and overall chemical stability. ML accelerates this process by extracting structure-
function relationships from large datasets and predicting opti- mal design configurations for specific catalytic reactions. For instance, Zhou et al. combined AI-based data mining with DFT calculations to reveal synergistic effects in multi- metallic MOFs, identifying Ni₃Fe₁-MOF as a superior oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalyst with an overpotential of just 208 mV (Fig. 12(a)). 181 This demonstrates how ML-guided screening can streamline multimetal catalyst discovery. Beyond OER catalysis, machine learning approaches have also been extensively applied to optimize MOF-based systems for carbon dioxide conversion. Li et al. employed multiple machines learning classifiers, including SVM, SGD, and neural networks, to predict the catalytic performance of MOFs in converting CO₂ to cyclic carbonates. 182 By training on experimental data and applying ensemble learning, they identified Mn, V, Cu, Ni, Zr,

2.4 Hybrid AI-simulation strategies First-principles calculations have long served as foundational tools in computational materials science, including the study of MOFs. Among them, density functional theory (DFT) is widely used for electronic structure analysis, bandgap calcula- tions, adsorption site identification, and reaction mechanism elucidation. 88
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations capture the time-evolution of atomic interactions, offering insights into the thermal stability, mechanical properties, and dynamic behavior of MOFs under various conditions. 89 Grand Canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulations, on the other hand, are indispensable for evaluating adsorption isotherms and gas uptake capacities by simulating gas–solid equilibria under varying pressures and temperatures. 90 These methods, though powerful and physically grounded, are often computationally intensive, especially when applied to large-scale screening across thousands of hypothetical or experimental MOF structures. To overcome the limitations of scale and computational cost associated with first-principles simulations, recent efforts have focused on integrating these methods with ML and AI frame- works. For instance, in the large-scale screening of hypothetical MOFs, simulation-derived data, such as adsorption energies from GCMC or structural descriptors from DFT, are used to train surrogate ML models, enabling rapid property prediction across expansive chemical spaces. Alternatively, MD simulations can first generate reliable datasets, which are then modeled using regression techniques to accelerate the evaluation of previously unexplored structures. These hybrid approaches effectively com- bine the physical rigor of simulation with the scalability of AI, opening new avenues for data-driven, simulation-informed MOF design. Specific case studies will be discussed in subsequent sections.

2.1.2 MOF databases and database subsets. Although com-
prehensive databases provide a wealth of crystallographic data, they are not specifically tailored for MOFs. Manually identifying and extracting MOF structures from resources like the CSD is a labor-intensive task, and this challenge is expected to intensify as the number of published structures continues to grow. 3 Consequently, using the entire database to train AI models is often impractical, prompting the development of MOF-specific curated subsets (as shown in Table 2). In 2012, Watanabe et al. extracted approximately 30 000 MOFs from CSD and conducted high-throughput screening studies for CO₂/N₂ separation. 40 In 2013, Goldsmith et al. extracted 38 800 metal–organic com- pounds from the CSD and subsequently generated 22 700 computable MOF samples for high-throughput screening of hydrogen storage. 41 In 2014, Chung et al. established the ‘‘Computation-Ready, Experimental MOFs’’ (CoRE MOF) data- base by mining the CSD for experimentally synthesized MOF structures. Through automated workflows, they removed both

text: phases, paving the way for the experimental realization of topo- logical insulators. 164 For example, Che et al. establishes a general inverse design strategy for 2D altermagnetic MOF monolayers by integrating Hu¨ckel theory-based nonbonding molecular orbital (NBMO) 165 analysis with first-principles calculations (Fig. 9(a)). By quantifying NBMO coefficients of organic ligands, the approach enables a symmetry-guided, data-informed framework that can be extended to machine-learning models for efficient discovery of spintronic MOFs with altermagnetic properties. Furthermore, a related theoretical study proposes a layer-mediated bilayer alter- magnet design strategy, demonstrating electric-field-tunable spin-splitting in bilayer MOFs through symmetry-guided screen- ing of spin point groups (Fig. 9(b)). 166 Very recently, Yue et al. developed a generalizable MLP for Zn-based MOFs using the data-efficient, equivariant nequIP architecture. 167 By train- ing on a curated dataset of DFT-augmented structures, the MLP accurately predicts forces, energies, and key physical properties across thousands of chemically diverse MOFs, which reduced the computational cost of high-throughput screening dramatically.

text:
4.1 Prediction of intrinsic MOF properties In MOF synthesis and design, ML and AI enables the analysis of large datasets to reveal structure–property relationships and predict material performance. AI-guided prediction of MOF properties has not only enhanced research productivity but also signaled a transformative shift from traditional trial-and- error methods toward data-centric materials discovery. This evolution is instrumental in tackling critical global challenges across energy, sustainability, and healthcare sectors. Key intrin- sic properties, including band gap, band structure, and charge distribution, among others, as critical intrinsic characteristics of MOFs, play a pivotal role in their applications, such as gas adsorption, separation, and catalysis.
4.1.1 Structural feature prediction. The topological and
pore structures of MOFs are critical to their performance, particularly in adsorption and separation processes. ML models trained on large, curated databases can effectively extract mean- ingful patterns from ligand and metal node information to predict structural features and related performance metrics. For instance, Michael Fernandez et al. reported the first ML model that classifies the performance of MOFs using only simple geometric features, aiming to capture carbon from power plant flue gases. 118 Wang et al. trained an ML model using a filtered dataset of 9156 MOFs from the hMOF database, with hydrogen adsorption capacities calculated via GCMC simulations (Fig. 6(a)). 119 By integrating MOF geometric descriptors (e.g., pore size, surface area) with MOFid and MOFkey encoding schemes, they successfully developed a pre- dictive model for hydrogen storage performance. Furthermore, the development of generative artificial intel- ligence tools has expanded the application boundaries for predicting the structural features of MOFs, moving beyond conventional predictive models based on known data. For example, tools such as GHP-MOF-assemble have enabled the automatic creation of virtual MOF libraries and the prediction of key structural parameters like surface area and porosity. These tools can further screen for candidates with high CO₂ adsorption capacities (42 mmol g 1 ) through molecular dynamics simulations (Fig. 6(b)). 120 Together, these examples illustrate how data-driven ML and generative AI models can accelerate the discovery of functional MOFs by mapping the relationship between structure and performance, thereby enabling rapid screening and design of novel candidates.
title: AI-driven advances in metal–organic frameworks: from data to design and applications

text:
4.2.2 Safety-related performance. AI-assisted prediction of
MOF functional properties has also extended into critical safety-related applications, such as flame retardancy and corro- sion resistance. These properties are inherently complex and difficult to quantify through conventional experiments alone due to their multivariate nature. AI offers advanced pattern recognition and multivariate analysis capabilities that enable precise modeling of nonlinear performance relationships. For instance, Zhang et al. demonstrates the power of AI/ML in accelerating the design of MOF-based polymeric nanocompo- sites by accurately predicting flame retardancy using a model trained on over 800 literature-derived data points. 141 Among five tested algorithms, the XGBoost model achieved the best performance (R² = 0.935), enabling experimental validation with only 6% prediction error and guiding further material optimization without the need for large-scale fire testing. In parallel, Anadebe et al. demonstrated the bifunctional role of Co-based MOFs as effective corrosion inhibitors for X65 steel in CO₂ environments, with strong agreement between experi- mental data and DFT/MD simulations, while an ANFIS model validates the predictive relationships for inhibition efficiency in practical pipeline protection (Fig. 7(i)–(k)). 142
title: AI-driven advances in metal–organic frameworks: from data to design and applications

text:
5.7 Biological applications MOFs formed by metal nodes and biocompatible ligands, enable efficient drug delivery and multimodal therapies by combining high loading capacity, controlled release, and unique imaging properties into a single nanoscale platform. Recent progress leveraging ML for predicting biocompatibility and optimizing functional properties has significantly expanded MOF applications in tissue engineering, gene delivery, and intelligent diagnostics. MOFs’ high specific surface area, tunable pore sizes, and multifunctional surfaces enable breakthroughs in drug delivery, overcoming challenges like low drug loading capacity and poor targeting. Menon et al. developed an ML-driven high-throughput screening framework by integrating over 35 000 organic toxicity datasets to build an interpretable random forest model with 81% accuracy in toxicity classification (Fig. 13(b)–(d)).
194 By combining this with metal toxicity data (LD50), they screened 86 000 MOFs from the Cambridge Structural Database, identifying 479 low- toxicity candidates. This study reveals key chemical descriptors, such as carbonyl oxygen count and drug-likeness index that govern toxicity, and proposes a porosity-biocompatibility trade- off. This ML framework accelerates rational design by reducing experimental risks and shortening development cycles, offering valuable chemical insights for synthesizing safe, targeted drug delivery MOFs. ML-driven MOF design also enables breakthroughs in dis- ease diagnosis and therapy. For example, Kibria’s team con- structed a diabetes prediction model using Random Forest and XGBoost algorithms, enhanced by SHAP interpretability analysis, achieving a balanced accuracy of 90%, thus providing a reliable, transparent clinical decision support tool. 196 In cancer therapy, the integration of AI with MOFs enables a new generation of personalized and adaptive treatment strategies. 197 AI enhances drug delivery efficiency, targeting precision, and real-time response assessment by analyzing extensive datasets on tumor characteristics, patient responses, and MOF behavior at the nano- bio interface. ML models, including GAN-based virtual screening, facilitate the intelligent design of MOF-based theragnostic platforms, while future integration with organ-on-a-chip systems may further accelerate clinical translation. 198,199 This AI-driven approach allows dynamic optimization of treatment plans, mini- mizing side effects and maximizing therapeutic outcomes.

text: utility of evaluating each candidate and identifies the most promising conditions for subsequent experiments. Candidates with either high predicted values or high predictive uncertainty are preferentially selected. After each evaluation, the surrogate model is updated with the new structure–property data, and the cycle is repeated until structures with optimal properties and low uncertainty are discovered. This strategy has already been successfully applied in nano- porous materials discovery. For instance, Deshwal et al. employed BO to screen B70 000 hypothetical COFs for methane adsorption performance. 106 By substantially reducing the number of time-consuming GCMC simulations, BO rapidly identified top- performing candidates. Remarkably, the optimal COF was found after only 140 simulations, recovering B30% of the top-100 candidates, whereas random search required 500 simulations to identify only the 170th-ranked structure. These results highlight the superior efficiency of BO-driven AL compared with conven- tional random or evolutionary search strategies in accelerating materials discovery. AL has also been applied to MOF research, ranging from the optimization of synthesis conditions to accelerating computa- tional screening. For example, a robotic platform was employed to rapidly synthesize ZIF-67 via Joule heating, with two tunable chemical parameters (precursor volume and molar ratio) and two process parameters (applied voltage and reaction time). 107 Using the data generated by the robotic system, a BO algorithm iteratively proposed new synthesis conditions. As the iterations progressed, the crystallinity of the obtained ZIF-67 gradually improved, ultimately yielding the target crystalline phase while significantly reducing the number of screening experiments, reaction time, and energy consumption. Beyond synthesis, BO has been further developed for MOF design and property optimization. Rajabi-Kochi et al. introduced the feature-adaptive Bayesian optimization (FABO) framework, which systematically integrates feature selection into the BO loop. 108 By dynamically identifying the most influential descriptors during each optimization cycle, FABO enables efficient MOF discovery without requiring prior knowl- edge of key features. Using the QMOF and CoRE-2019 datasets, FABO successfully identified the top-performing MOFs for CO₂ adsorption and bandgap prediction within only 135 iterations, recovering over 20% of the top-100 candidates. Given the enormous design space of MOFs, exhaustive simulation or experimental evaluation is impractical. To address this, Comlek et al. proposed the latent variable Gaussian process with multi- objective batch Bayesian optimization (LVGP-MOBBO) frame- work (Fig. 5(b)). 109 Unlike conventional BO methods that rely on explicit physical descriptors, LVGP-MOBBO leverages quali- tative building-block representations to perform global optimi- zation. Remarkably, by exploring only B1% of the design space, the method successfully identified all Pareto-front solu- tions and over 97% of the top-50 candidates for CO₂ uptake and CO₂/N₂ selectivity. Compared with random forest models, LVGP demonstrated superior robustness and interpretability, as the latent variables provided physically meaningful insights into MOF design principles. More recently, Liu et al. combined
title: AI-driven advances in metal–organic frameworks: from data to design and applications

text: traditional BO with the Vendi score, an interpretable diversity measure, to balance exploration and exploitation in MOF discovery. 110 By learning from a mixed database of B10 000 MOFs, the algorithm identified twelve experimental and eight hypothetical MOFs with optimal designs for NH₃ storage. A recent study by Dobbelaere et al. has pushed the boundary of AL for MOFs and developed a ‘‘cluster-based’’ learning methodology to build machine learning potentials (MLP) that accurately model spatial defects in large, disordered MOF systems comprising tens of thousands of atoms (Fig. 5(c) and (d)). 111 The key idea is to extract local chemical environ- ments as finite molecular fragments (‘‘clusters’’) from bulk MOF structures, feed them into MLP training, and selectively augment the training dataset where the model shows high uncertainty. By requiring significantly fewer ab initio reference data points, this AL-like workflow balances computational cost with accuracy, enabling the resultant potentials to reproduce the mechanical properties of disordered UiO-66-derived struc- tures with near-quantum mechanical fidelity. Recent advances in NLP and LLMs have further expanded the scope and efficiency of AL in MOF research by broadening the accessible initial datasets beyond curated databases to the vast body of scientific literature. 112 Early attempts relied on text- mining algorithms to autonomously extract feedback from exist- ing data; for instance, Nandy et al. employed NLP and image recognition to retrieve solvent stability and thermal degradation information for MOFs directly from experimental reports. 113 Subsequent studies extended this approach to the extraction of synthetic conditions from procedural texts, thereby enhancing the understanding of synthesis strategies. 55 More recently, LLMs have emerged as indispensable tools for literature-driven data mining, offering higher flexibility and accuracy than rule-based methods in parsing complex scientific knowledge. 114 Notably, Yaghi’s group introduced the GPT-4 Reticular Chemist framework, which performs MOF design and planning entirely through natural language interfaces without requiring coding, 87,115 while Kang and Kim’s ChatMOF integrated semantic retrieval from databases such as CoRE MOF and QMOF with generative modeling to predict properties and design novel MOFs with targeted function- alities (Fig. 5(e)). 56 When coupled with AL workflows, these LLM- enabled data extraction approaches not only expand the diversity of training datasets but also provide dynamic, literature-informed feedback loops, ultimately accelerating and refining the discovery of functional MOFs. AL offers a powerful paradigm shift for MOF discovery by introducing closed-loop, feedback-driven exploration that goes beyond conventional forward or inverse design strategies. This capability not only accelerates discovery but also expands the exploration space beyond established design heuristics, thereby fostering opportunities for uncovering unconventional MOF structures and properties. 116,117 Recent applications demon- strate the versatility of AL in addressing both experimental and computational challenges. The integration of NLP and large language models further broadens its impact by coupling literature-driven knowledge extraction with iterative optimiza- tion workflows. To navigate and operate efficiently in dynamic environments, these robots employ high- precision localization and mapping methods, including SLAM, 27,51 six-point localization (for pose determination), 27 ArUco labels (for visual marker tracking) 52 and so on. Robotic systems are seamlessly integrated with automation soware and real-time feedback mechanisms, enabling the optimization of experimental workows and signicantly enhancing reproducibility. 60,61 When combined with automated workstations, these systems can execute complex, dexterous experiments and manage entire workows—spanning synthesis, characterization, and testing—with minimal human intervention. For instance, Lunt et al. 28 designed a solid-state workow incorporating a PXRD instrument, two grinding stations, and a Chemspeed liquid dispensing platform to conduct PXRD experiments efficiently. Similarly, Cooper et al. 27 developed a robotic system with eight workstations to identify photocatalyst mixtures for hydrogen production, ultimately achieving formulations six times more active than the initial ones. Further advancing the eld, Zhu et al. 52 implemented a system with fourteen workstations, featuring dedicated regions for auto-synthesis, auto-characterization, and auto- performance testing. This comprehensive system enables fully automated experimental processes, accelerating catalyst discovery and optimization.

2.2 Large-scale intelligent model Interpretable predictive models and advanced algorithms are crucial components of the autonomous laboratory workow. They enable efficient data processing, accurate outcome prediction, and informed decision-making at each experi- mental stage. By leveraging data from previous experiments, predictive models can forecast the results of proposed experi- ments more effectively. For instance, in a study by Moosavi et al., 45 involving genetic algorithm (GA)-guided robotic plat- form optimized crystallinity and phase purity in metal–organic frameworks, they explored a nine-parameter space through 90 experiments across three generations. A random forest model, trained iteratively on prior data, predicted outcomes and
excluded experiments likely to yield suboptimal results. GAs⁴⁶ are particularly effective for handling large numbers of variables and are widely applied in the discovery of novel catalysts and 47,48 their synthesis optimization. 49 Beyond GAs, the SNOBFIT algorithm improves search effi- ciency by combining local and global search strategies. It has been successfully applied₅₀to optimize chemical reactions in continuous ow reactors. Another widely used method in autonomous laboratories is Bayesian optimization, which minimizes 27,31,51 the – number 53 of trials needed to achieve convergence. The performance of Bayesian optimization is highly dependent on the choice of the surrogate model, with Gaussian processes (GPs) and random forests (RFs) being the 20,54 most common for regression tasks. The Phoenics algorithm, based on the Bayesian neural network 55 (BNN), achieves faster convergence than GPs and RFs. It has been integrated into ChemOS (a versatile soware package) for several automated platforms, including 53 the Ada self-driving laboratory for thin- lm 27 materials, and a mobile robotic chemist by Burger et al. for optimizing aqueous photocatalysts. Alongside advanced algorithms, another critical aspect of optimizing workows for intelligent models is the iterative experiment-theory feedback loop. Automated theoretical 56,57 calculations, such as density functional theory (DFT), provide valuable prior knowledge and bridge the gap between theory and experiment. This data fusion enhances adaptive learning capabilities, allowing models to continuously update and rene their predictions. As a result, these intelligent models drive the 51,52 development of closed-loop iterative automation processes.

3.2 Iterative autonomous experiments driven by a computational ‘brain’ The automated platform driven by iterative algorithms is essentially a black-box optimization technique that uses experimental data for training to obtain the relationship between design variables and the observed values of the objective function, thereby enabling learning and decision- making. This optimization process lacks systematic prior knowledge and has low efficiency in exploring chemical space, and the interpretability of the optimization results is poor.
48 As an essential tool for comprehending molecular behavior and forecasting chemical properties, computational chemistry is ideally suited for prior knowledge in optimization procedures. Computational chemistry can greatly increase the speed and scalability of chemical space exploration by incorporating machine learning. 76 First-principles computational simulations can obtain microscopic information that is difficult to acquire in the real world, such as adsorption energy and electronic structures. The macroscopic properties of materials oen depend on their microscopic characteristics. Therefore, combining machine learning models with rst-principles calculations can provide pre-trained models and theoretical support for experiments, thereby guiding the experimental process and accelerating the iteration of materials. Yin et al. 77 established an approach that utilizes ML-accelerated theoretical calculations, enabling collaboration between experiments and theory for screening small-sized ordered alloy catalysts. By calculating the solubility and chemical ordering of a third metal element in a PtCo ordered alloy system, as well as the adsorption of related intermediates, they found that the introduction of Cu or Ni into the PtCo alloy is benecial for the thermodynamic driving force to transition from disorder to order. In contrast, the introduc- tion of Mn and Fe inhibits the disorder-to-order transition of the alloy. Moreover, the synthesized PtCoNi and PtCoCu alloys exhibited excellent oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) perfor- mance. This makes it possible to quickly discover potential ordered alloys with high thermodynamic driving force and good performance from the vast design space. Zhang et al. used high-throughput DFT calculations to obtain the formation energy Efand surface stress 3surfof high-entropy intermetallic compounds (HEICs) with different compositions. Based on the

To date, the number of research elds integrated with AI are rapidly evolving and hold immense untapped potential. An effective AI-driven approach relies on large amounts of high-quality, structured data as its foundation to develop robust prediction models. However, the majority of available data, particularly experimental data, suffers from signicant issues such as non-standardization, fragmentation, and poor repro- ducibility. 20,21 In this context, automated robotic platforms are being rapidly developed to generate high-quality experimental data in a standardized and high-throughput manner while minimizing manual effort. 22–25 More importantly, these plat- forms can fully leverage their advantages when integrated with AI algorithms. Such integration not only automates routine tasks but also enables complex decision-making processes, optimization of synthesis methods, and even planning of experimental workows. 15,25–31 A pioneering study was con- ducted by Cooper et al., 27 who developed a mobile chemist capable of autonomously conducting high-throughput photo- catalyst selection, outperforming humans through the appli- cation of Bayesian optimization. By simulating the sintering kinetics of these metal support pairs, they discovered that the sintering kinetics exhibit a Sabatier principle with respect to MSI. They also found that the sintering initiation temperature of metal NPs with appropriate MSI is about half of the bulk metal melting temperature of typical NPs (∼3 nm), which is consistent with the long-reported empirical Tammann temperature. In addition, based on the revealed Sabatier principle and scaling relationships, high-throughput screening of carrier combinations with different energies was conducted, resulting in carriers that increase the sintering temperature. This has greatly advanced the design of ultra- stable supported metal NP catalysts. 3.3 End-to-end intelligent autonomous systems powered by large-scale models The overall input-to-output nature of machine learning methods can form a powerful single-purpose tool, capable of quickly generating experimental plans and obtaining optimal experimental solutions. However, the goal of fully autonomous end-to-end synthesis reaction design and development is still to be achieved. First, an end-to-end intelligent automation plat- form requires a large-scale model with strong generalization ability and wide applicability. It is difficult to achieve ML methods trained solely on data obtained from theoretical
calculations and experiments. The emergence of LLMs based on ChatGPT tools in 2022 has made such large-scale models possible. Agent-based LLMs can accommodate vast amounts of knowledge and information and possess strong human– computer interaction capabilities, enabling them to make ex- ible decisions based on complex and non-standardized inputs. Researchers have also developed large-scale models tailored for chemistry to enhance reasoning capabilities in autonomous laboratories. For example, SynAsk, an LLM-powered organic chemistry platform created by AIChemEco Inc., was presented by Zhang et al. 86 Through domain-specic data renement and integration with a chain-of-thought methodology, SynAsk provides easy access to advanced chemical tools and a compre- hensive knowledge base in a question-and-answer style (Fig. 4a). A basic chemistry knowledge base, molecular information retrieval, reaction performance prediction, retrosynthesis prediction, and chemical literature acquisition are some of the features offered by this platform. This creative approach creates a paradigm unique to organic chemistry that makes research and discoveries in the eld easier by integrating external resources with ne-tuning procedures. Moreover, a complete chemical experiment workow typi- cally includes three stages: synthesis, characterization, and performance testing. AgFeO₂ (dynamic transmittance range: 40–80%) and electro- magnetic shielding capability of AgCrO₂ (430 dB) can be integrated to create interfaces with dual-mode dynamic dim- ming and EMI suppression. 29,206 Defect-engineered CuCrO₂ nanoparticle electrodes exhibit rapid response (o10 ms), while gradient buffer layers formed through atomic interdiffusion enhance structural stability during flexural operation. 206 Display integration techniques now exploit solution- processable delafossite nanocrystals for scalable fabrication. Hydrothermal-synthesized CuGaO₂ nanoplates form dense, pin-hole-free films for cathodes in p-type dye-sensitized solar cells (p-DSSCs), achieving saturation photovoltages 4460 mV, 83 while core–shell heterojunctions (e.g., CuFeO₂@Cu₂O) boost photocurrent density by 300%. 71 Future breakthroughs hinge on mitigating wide-bandgap limitations (e.g., via Mg doping to extend absorption to 500 nm) and optimizing inter- facial charge transfer in stacked QLED architectures. 2 Despite significant advances, key challenges remain: enhancing the conductivity of undoped CuCrO₂ (currently B10 2 Scm¹) and optimizing interfacial stress control in flexible devices to accelerate full-color flexible display commercialization. 241 Future research should prioritize: (1) band engineering to optimize carrier transport/optical absorption balance; (2) atomic-scale interface control techniques; and (3) advanced manufacturing processes like roll-to-roll printing. These approaches will accelerate the commercial deployment of dela- fossite materials in AR displays and wearable electronics.

5.3 Research gaps and challenges Despite revolutionary potential, scalable implementation of ABO₂ delafossites faces bottlenecks across the synthesis- property-device integration chain, compounded by fundamental knowledge gaps in physical mechanisms, extreme-environment responses, and cross-domain synergy. Current progress remains concentrated on specific systems (e.g.,CuGaO2and AgFeO₂), with material system imbalances and foundational knowledge limitations constraining transformative advances.
5.3.1 Technical bottlenecks: core barriers from synthesis
to integration. (1) Synthesis limitations include elemental segregation during high-temperature solid-state reactions (4800 1C, e.g., 415% impurity phases in CuFeO₂ from uncon- trolled Fe 3+ /Fe 2+ ratios) and solvent residue limiting solution- processed film conductivities to o10 S cm 1. Epitaxial growth of noble metal systems (e.g., PtCoO₂) suffers from thermal decomposition, with grain boundary densities reaching 10 6 cm 2 and conductivities 2–3 orders below single crystals. The cost disparity between vapor deposition equipment and solution-based wafer-scale precision control exacerbates man- ufacturing challenges.

2.3.3 Charge density wave: synergistic control of strong
electronic correlation and photoelectronic response. The inter- play between strong electronic correlations and charge density waves (CDWs) in delafossite materials reveals unique quantum control capabilities, directly linked to emergent topological phenomena. In PdCrO₂ and PdCoO₂, for instance, strong correlations within the CrO₂ layers induce localized charge- ordered states, while the noble metal layers (Pd) maintain near- free-electron characteristics. DFT+DMFT calculations confirm that this interlayer decoupling causes anomalous Fermi velocity enhancement (8.2 10 5 ms¹) and hidden metal–metal transitions. 16,75,121,140 Crucially, CDW formation correlates with topological phase transitions: In materials like PdCrO₂, CDW modulation drives a transition from conventional insu- lator to topological insulator, accompanied by Berry-phase accumulation and emergence of topologically protected surface states. Further, in infinite-layer nickelates (e.g., NdNiO₂), four- fold rotational symmetry breaking facilitates Ni-3d/Nd-5d orbi- tal hybridization, forming CDWs via Ni–Nd–Ni antiferromag- netic superexchange channels. 141–144 Fermi surface nesting on polar cleavage planes triggers two-dimensional incommensu- rate CDW modulation, forming a 3.2 nm period moire´ super- lattice (wave vector Q₁ = 0.32 Å 1 ), with STM revealing a periodic charge modulation amplitude of 32%. 145 Experimen- tally, a double-peaked energy gap of 18 meV near the Fermi level is confirmed on the PdCrO₂ surface, where many-body interactions significantly modulate carrier transport. Theoretical studies indicate that an orbital-selective Mott transition in the CrO₂ layer triggers CDW order when the correlation strength U 4 4.5 eV. 16,140 Layer-resolved standing-wave X-ray photoelec- tron spectroscopy (SW-XPS) confirms that anisotropic CDW modulation in PdCoO₂ is induced by cross-layer coupling between Pd layer plasmon excitations and charge-transfer excita- tions in the CoO₂ layer. 105,107,140 The stability of this CDW is synergistically enhanced by antiferromagnetic ordering, with topological protection mechanisms significantly suppressing order parameter fluctuations. 4.5.1 Transparent conductive devices. Performance enhance-
ment of delafossite-based TCOs necessitates co-optimization of electrical properties and optical transmittance. At the materials level, Mg/Ni co-doped CuCrO₂ (s =1.6Scm¹, 63% visible transmittance) significantly enhances hole mobility through valence band delocalization, 5 while Rh-doped CuRhO₂ achieves s =735Scm 1 with 85% near-infrared transmittance, surpassing traditional p-type TCO limitations in infrared regimes. 110 Fabrication-wise, RF sputtering combined with 600 1C annealing optimizes crystallinity and surface roughness in CuCrO₂ films, whereas ultrasonic spray pyrolysis enables solution-processed conductivities exceeding 100 S cm 1. 8,186 Nevertheless, competi- tive effects between oxygen interstitials and cation vacancies continue to constrain mobility (o1cm² V 1 s 1 ). 122 Architectural innovations center on heterojunction band engineering: p-CuScO₂/ n-In₂O₃ heterostructures reduce threshold voltages to 2.5 V through type-II band alignment while suppressing interfacial recombination, 122 but CuAlO₂/4H-SiC Schottky diodes exhibit exceptional interface quality with rectification ratios up to 10 6. 187 Persistent challenges include intrinsic hole mobility limitations and low-temperature process compatibility. Future advances require enhancing valence band delocalization through 4d metal co-doping and developing atomic layer deposition (ALD) techni- ques (o250 1C) for flexible electronics integration. 110,122

text: photo(electro)catalysis. 62–64 Machine learning-guided high- pressure hydrothermal synthesis has expanded compositional diversity to 4100 material systems. 9,65 The layered architecture of delafossite materials enables high-performance heterostructures. Weak interlayer bonding (5–30 meV) allows exfoliation or epitaxy to construct mono- layers (e.g., 1.2–1.8 nm CuFeO₂ exhibiting out-of-plane ferroe- lectricity). Heterojunctions with 2D materials (e.g., 495% lattice-matched CuGaO₂/MoS₂) enhance band bending (con- duction band offset: 0.38 eV), boosting the carrier separation efficiency by 420-fold. 67–71 Core–shell structures (CuRhO₂@- CuGaO₂) achieve near-complete pollutant degradation via Z- scheme charge transfer (built-in field 410 3 Vcm 1 ). 10 Critically, delafossites exhibit exceptional defect tolerance: covalently bonded [BO₆] layers alternating with ionic A + layers localize defects via weak van der Waals interactions (binding energy: 5–30 meV). Low-energy interlayer sliding barriers (o0.5 eV) accommodate local distortions without macroscopic degradatio- n—unlike perovskites (e.g.,MAPbI₃), where ionic migration causes device failure. 72,73 This stability originates from the [BO₆]frame- work’s distortion buffering; CuFeO₂ retains phase purity even with 12% excess Cu/O. 67,74 Tolerance mechanisms include: intrinsic defect suppression (PdCoO₂ impurity o100 ppm), doping adapt- ability (Zn-doped CuCrO₂ achieves 220 mWm 1 K 2 power factor), and dynamic stability (covalent bonds inhibit ion migration at high T). 19,53,73,75–78 The features of layered structure and polytypes of delafossite materials provide ideal platforms for quantum phenomena. AgFeO₂ exhibits spin-polarization-dependent 2H–3R transitions, enabling ferro-/antiferromagnetic switching. 31 Extreme anisotro- pic magnetoresistance in nonmagnetic layered metals reveals Lorentz-force-driven disruption of interlayer coherence. 79 Quan- tum confinement in PdCoO₂ yields spin coherence lengths (22.4 nm), exceeding spin precession lengths. 80 Negative long- itudinal magnetoresistance in PdCoO₂/PtCoO₂ arises from Fermi-point anomalies at Yamaji angles. 81 These phenomena underpin spin valves and Majorana zero modes while advancing research on emergent quantum states. In summary, delafossite structural features—quasi-2D superlattices, polytypic synergy, and compositional tunability— establish a multidimensional framework for photoelectronic design. Intrinsic anisotropy governs light absorption and carrier transport, while A/B-site substitution enables precise property control. Superior defect tolerance outperforms perovskites in stability, and weak interlayer bonding facilitates heterojunction engineering. Furthermore, disordered doping creates high- entropy systems, whereas ordered doping forms honeycomb/ kagome lattices (Table 1) for topological electronics. These struc- tural merits synergize with photoelectronic functionality, cement- ing the role of delafossite materials in energy conversion and quantum technologies.

site materials are crucial for achieving selective gas sensing. 4.3 Multidimensional breakthroughs and innovative applications of quantum control Quantum control has emerged as a pivotal strategy for over- coming the photoelectronic performance limits of delafossite materials. Their inherent layered structure, low-dimensional characteristics, and rich many-body interactions provide a unique platform for targeted manipulation of quantum effects. From quantum confinement-induced band renormalization to spin splitting and Berry phase effects modulated through inter- face engineering, and extending to the synergy between ballistic transport and spectral conversion, the quantum behavior of these materials exhibits intricate multidimensional coupling. This control paradigm not only significantly optimizes critical parameters such as light absorption, carrier transport, and energy conversion efficiency but also enables novel applications in high-mobility transparent conductors, spintronic devices, and photoelectronic-magnetic coupling systems. Quantum confinement effects enable precise reconstruction of bandgaps, carrier effective masses, and transport pathways via dimensional engineering (e.g., 3D bulk - 2D nanosheets/ 1D nanowires). A representative example is CuGaO₂ nanosheets, where surface polarization generates a built-in electric field that effectively promotes photogenerated carrier separation, with photocurrent density exhibiting linear correlation with nanosheet aspect ratio. 290
In KCrSe₂, an incommensurately modulated struc- ture formed through interlayer atomic rearrangement induces strong quantum confinement, elevating the magnetic transition temperature by 1.6–3.3 times. 290 Particularly notable are CuFeO₂ nanosheets: thickness reduction below 5 nm expands the band- gap from the bulk value of 1.56 eV to 2.20 eV, significantly enhancing UV response capability. 173,230,291 This effect also boosts the incident photon-to-electron conversion efficiency (IPCE) of CuFeO₂ and CuGaO₂ by 200% within the visible spectrum, open- ing new pathways for photocatalysis and photovoltaics. 11,68 Interface quantum engineering offers innovative solutions for spin-polarized transport. Within PdCrO₂ heterostructures, interfacial strong spin–orbit coupling induces Rashba spin splitting as large as 200 meV Å, yielding spin polarization transport efficiency far exceeding that of conventional 2D materials. 128 Symmetry breaking further triggers unconven- tional Hall effects and topological transport behaviors, laying foundations for quantum information devices. 27,128,138 Experi- mental studies confirm that a r1 monolayer CuCrO₂ buffer layer effectively suppresses defect density in epitaxial PdCrO₂ films (STEM/EELS characterization o10 10 cm 2 ) while preser- ving hexagonal lattice symmetry, significantly enhancing car- rier mobility. 73,128 The observation of micrometer-scale (41 mm) electron mean free paths in ultra-pure PdCoO₂

text: The full integration of sustainable technologies to combat climate change heavily depends on the discovery of cost-competitive, safe, and durable performative materials, specifically for electrochemical systems that can generate energy, store energy, and produce chemicals. Due to the vast exploration space, scientists have adapted high throughput methods, both computational and experimental, for screening, synthesis, and testing to accelerate material discovery. In this review, we analyze such high throughput methodologies reported in the literature that have been applied to electrochemical material discovery. We find that most reported studies utilize computational methods, including density functional theory and machine learning, over experimental methods. Some labs have combined computational and experimental methods to create powerful tools for a closed loop material discovery process through automated setups and machine learning. Either way, over 80% of the publications we reviewed focus on catalytic materials, revealing a shortage in high throughput ionomer, membrane, electrolyte, and substrate material research. Moreover, we find that most material screening criteria do not consider cost, availability, and safety, all of which are crucial properties when assessing the economic feasibility of proposed materials. In addition, we discover that high throughput electrochemical material discovery in a handful of countries, revealing the global opportunity to collaborate and share resources and data for further acceleration of material discovery. The accelerating climate crisis and rising energy demands require sustainable electrochemical technologies for energy storage, generation, and chemical production. Over the past two decades, electrochemical technologies have gained much attention due to improved material and reactor performance and new material discovery, propelling commercialization and scale-up. However, key performance benchmarks (e.g., activity, selectivity, and energy efficiency) still need to be achieved before such emerging technologies can compete economically with existing fossil fuel-based processes. 9–13 Material bottlenecks— such as cost, durability, and scalability, continue to limit progress. For example, precious metal catalysts such as plat- inum, gold, and iridium are still state of the art for many elec- trochemical reactions. At the same time, the substrates, ionomers, membranes, and electrolytes used in the reactors degrade over long-term operation, posing signicant chal- lenges. text: of ML makes it a powerful tool for creating new solutions to computational materials discovery. In recent years, the use of generative AI models (large language models, diffusion models, reinforcement learning- based generative models, etc.) in materials design has been on the rise. Yet, generative AI is still limited to applications in academia and research as evidence of its applications in industry or production/manufacturing environments is lacking. In research applications, scientists have applied generative AI to aid in materials discovery. For example, Song et al. and Li et al. applied inverse material design via ML to synthesize materials with specic properties for electrochemical CO₂ reduction or high-capacity energy storage, respectively. 82,83 Moreover, Alver- son et al. utilized generative AI models such as variational auto- encoders, generative adversarial networks, and genetic algo- rithms as use cases for creating crystals and proposing new structures. 84 Additionally, Bang, Kim, Hong et al. expanded on inverse design using generative AI models to discover materials with multiple properties, rather than optimizing a single property. 85 While generative AI in materials discovery shows promise in limited applications in electrochemical materials discovery, it shares many of the pain points seen in other ML methods, such as a lack of publicly available robust training datasets and the limited ability of models to generalize outside of training dataset distributions and to real world experimentation. While ML is a powerful tool that helps improve the quality and efficiency of the HT materials discovery process in many ways, it comes with drawbacks and challenges. First, insuffi- cient high-quality data impede training accurate, generalizable machine learning models. 86 Data-intensive ML models such as NNs and RFR require large, information-dense datasets for suitable performance. Creating datasets from experimental work, especially when traversing all possibilities of a material database, is demanding as experiments are expensive and time- consuming, require highly skilled experts, and are oen proprietary. A lack of quality data can lead to poor model predictions when exploring beyond a model's training dataset distributions. Second, integrating multiple data sources (such as experimental work and DFT simulations) to train ML models lacks standardization, making collaborative efforts to solve problems in the eld more challenging. 87 Third, many ML algorithms behave as a “black box”, making their predictions challenging to trust and their proposed structure–property relationships impossible to explain explicitly. Nevertheless, these challenges can be addressed by building more robust and interpretive models and placing an emphasis on standardizing data handling practices. 87

3.3 Other notable efforts Many material deposition methods listed in Table 2 involve a liquid phase by which the material is rst formulated into an ink, solution, or dispersion (e.g., drop-casting and spray coating). Sputtering, a type of physical vapor deposition, is another common method for depositing metal particles, specically, but does not require rst dispersing the metal in a solvent. The advantages of sputtering include greater control of particle size, composition, thickness, and loading than wet deposition methods, and it is possible to create compositional libraries with this technique.
141 As an alternative to sputtering and other deposition methods, a Dutch company, VSParticle, designed a nano-printer for printing (semi)conductive particles. This innovative technology, depicted in Fig. 5, employs spark ablation followed by impaction to form and deposit nano- particles. 110,124 While sputtering typically requires the target material and a high-energy ion source by way of ionizing Ar to Ar +, spark ablation only requires the target metal, electricity, and an inert gas and thus is a “chemical-free” deposition. With adjustable parameters such as voltage, current, ow rate, and nozzle size, this nano-printer boasts the ability to make highly tunable nanoparticle lms of varying compositions, thick- nesses, loadings, and particle sizes in a matter of hours. In fact, Becker et al. printed 64 (8 × 8) NiFe electrodes of various compositions to test in their customized cell, with each elec- trode only taking 1–320 seconds to print. 124 In a different study, Sapountzi et al. fabricated IrO₂-coated membranes using spark ablation for conducting the OER at a h of the loading (cost) compared to commercially available catalyst coated membranes 110 (CCMs), underscoring the importance of the deposition method when designing cost-competitive materials. The materials listed in Table 2 have potential for use in a myriad of electrochemical applications, yet most were studied at the lab scale. If a certain catalyst or electrolyte, for example, proves performative and cost-effective, then the next step would be scaling up its production. Zhang et al. took that next step by reporting HT production of two-dimensional MoS₂ akes for fabricating thermally treated MoS₂/Mo₂C (HC–MoS₂/Mo₂C) catalyst for the HER. 105 The reported method involved extracting raw Mo concentrates (MoS₂, MoO₂, MoO₃, and others) from an active open pit mine and exfoliating it with Mo₂C to form two- dimensional MoS₂ akes. 2.1.5 Limitations and considerations in computational
methods. While theoretical calculations have enabled signi- cant advances in electrochemical materials discovery, several fundamental limitations affect their application in high- throughput screening. 88 First, accuracy-efficiency trade-offs are inherent to all computational methods. DFT functional selec- tion signicantly impacts results, with different functionals yielding distinct trends that can affect screening outcomes. Second, reaction condition complexity presents major chal- lenges, as electrochemical processes involve multiple variables (electrolytes, pH, applied potentials, temperature, etc.) that are computationally expensive to model explicitly. Many studies rely on simplied models that may not capture realistic oper- ating conditions, such as using DFT energies rather than free energies, which are unable to obtain energetics at experimental temperatures. Third, kinetic limitations are oen overlooked, as most screening approaches use thermodynamic descriptors rather than kinetic parameters, potentially missing important rate-determining factors and complex reaction mechanisms. Finally, transferability issues arise when force elds or ML models trained on specic systems are applied to broader materials classes without adequate validation. Data reproducibility remains a major bottleneck in compu- tational materials discovery. Experiments from which training datasets are derived may have similar product compositions but differ in the structure or properties due to changes in process parameters. Reproducibility can be improved by thorough capture of metadata and tracking key information such as ingredient lots, sample storage conditions, equipment calibra- tion logs, etc. Initiatives such as the Materials Genome Initia- tive, Materials Acceleration Platform, and, for computational datasets, Novel Materials Discovery aim to improve reproduc- ibility by hosting datasets that have detailed metadata, thus

Understanding that the search space for catalyst multi- element electrocatalysts is too vast even for automated HT robotic platforms, Kodera and Sayama also incorporated ML into their robot system to explore catalysts for the OER and HClO production using seawater. 153 Their fully automatic robot was able to conduct synthesis and electroanalysis of 88 catalyst samples per day. The authors started by setting their system to synthesize and analyze different combinations of four elements (Co, Mn, Fe, and Ni), chosen based on their reported perfor- mance, to obtain 286 data entries. With these data, the authors investigated composition optimization using BO by having the ML model and robot run cycles; the model suggested 10 mate- rials which the robot system then synthesized and analyzed. The cycles were halted aer four loops when the model identi- ed the top 10 performing materials of the 286 original samples. Thus, only 40 samples were needed to validate and optimize the model. The authors stress that, as stated in the previous paragraph, BO-guided experiments reduce the time needed to evaluate datasets and optimize materials. In addi- tion, the authors proposed choosing more elements, expanding the abilities of their robot platform, and using multi-objective optimization such as that by Kavalsky et al. 57

3. Experimental methods The methodology for most experimental electrochemical tests involves material synthesis or preparation, material deposition or casting, electroanalysis, and pre- and post-testing charac- terization. The step-by-step process very much depends on the reaction and the type of material being tested. Therefore, unlike computational studies, setups across labs can vary vastly, leading to many customized setups for both benchtop and HT experimentation. While insightful, this variety in experimental setups hinders data comparison across research labs. Yet, researchers thoroughly detailing their methods and custom setups in publications stimulate more similarities as others incorporate proven procedures into their own setups. Mean- while, continuous efforts to commercialize HT experimental setups will drive method standardization, thus minimizing differences in procedures from lab to lab. 3.4 Analytical characterization Physical characterization performed before and aer electro- analysis plays an imperative role in scientic methods of HT material discovery. Researchers incorporate analytical charac- terization (morphology, composition, crystallization, etc.)in traditional benchtop studies to answer questions about a material's performance. Thus, HT experimental methods also require HT characterization techniques to identify the most feasible materials for electrochemical applications. Scientists have innovated new techniques to address speed-related bottlenecks in common analytical methods such as X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray uorescence.
142,143 Incorporating multi-sample and automated stages into instruments increases the number of samples that can be characterized while reducing analysis time. Parallel chambers in systems for Fourier- transform infrared spectroscopy, ultraviolet-visible spectros- copy, and N₂ adsorption/desorption allow for samples to be loaded and analyzed simultaneously. Various labs [and manu- facturers] have also employed robotic arms for machine tending to automate menial measurements such as mass loading to increase process efficiency. 144 Machine manufacturers for these common techniques have already rolled out their HT versions of their instruments. 145–148 Taking it a step further, researchers have gone so far as to start incorporating ML into physical characterization techniques to improve their efficacy. Szy- manski et al. developed an autonomous and adaptive XRD by coupling ML with a physical diffractor to hasten phase detec- tion, leading to in situ identication of short-lived intermediates during solid-state reactions. 149 This application serves as a nice segue into the following section where we discuss combined computational and experimental methods.

text: Within the larger class of SPM, scanning electrochemical microscopy (SECM) is a complex technique used to evaluate local electrochemical behavior at interfaces such as liquid/solid, liquid/gas, and liquid/liquid. 270-277 When this method was initially created in 1989, 278 it completely changed the discipline of electrochemistry by making it possible to conduct in-depth, spatially resolved electrochemical investigations. text: topography that can couple into the measured signals. These effects are especially significant for the contact mode methods. For SPM-based mechanical measurements and conductive measurements, signal scales with the contact area. 353, 354 For PFM the fundamental signal is independent of topography; 355 however, secondary couplings due to the changes in the resonance frequency of the cantilever are possible. 191 For the non-contact methods, topography can couple to the measured signal via the gradients of the capacitive forces. 356-358 However, these effects are considerably weaker for the detection signals based on differential signals such as photovoltage measurements. Correspondingly, the key task for the SPM-based materials discovery is the quantification and deconvolution of topographic effects. This can be accomplished via instrument-based strategies such as probe calibration, correction methodologies, or sample design. The calibration of the probe is the first step on the way to decoupling the target response from the topography impact. The complexity of this task arises from multiple factors. Firstly, the observed topographical signal is a result of a convolution between the tip with unknown geometry and the unknown topographical features of the sample surface (“blind deconvolution”). Changes in the tip geometry – due to uncontrolled degradation, contamination, or other factors – introduce alterations in the observable signal. In the case of "blind deconvolution," isolating true surface features from artifacts introduced by the evolving condition of the tip during scanning is particularly challenging. Another complication arises from the mechanical nature of the SPM detection system. The interaction of the probe with the surface is inherently nonlinear due to the finite hardness of the surface, which often varies within a single scan, adhesion forces, surface adsorbates, and contamination, water meniscus in the tip-surface contact, etc. These variations are also reflected in the measured signal. From a technical point of view, the radical solution for the probe calibration can be achieved by integrating scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and SPM microscopy. In a ‘fusion scope’ a single surface region can be sequentially examined by both methods yielding complementary data that enhance calibration accuracy. SEM can also be used to monitor the condition of the probe, allowing for direct observation of its changes throughout the experimental process. Another approach for achieving artifact-free SPM measurements lies in developing advanced methods that account for multiple influencing factors observed in various SPM experiments. While capturing the target functionality from a single measurement is challenging, complementary data from multiple SPM experiments can help isolate the target signal from topographical crosstalk. section_title_original: IV.d. Surface photovoltage measurements by Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy
text: improved the design and optimization of various materials, including perovskites, organic photovoltaics, traditional silicon cells, and diverse photocatalytic systems like plasmonic photocatalysts. 307-309 KPFM, first introduced by Nonnenmacher in 1991, 310 operates by measuring variations in the local contact potential difference (CPD) under ambient conditions. This CPD reflects the difference in Fermi levels between the tip and the sample. The mapping of CPD is performed using a conductive tip positioned slightly above the sample surface. An AC voltage is applied to the tip and the electrostatic response is tracked using a lock-in amplifier. This approach enables two different detection methods: amplitude modulation (AM) mode and frequency modulation (FM) mode. In AM mode, the method tracks variations in the response amplitude. An additional DC voltage (UDC) is applied to the tip to achieve accurate measurements. The electrostatic force is minimized when UDC equals the UCPD between the tip and the sample. This condition, UDC = UCPD, ensures precise mapping of the surface potential. The FM mode lies in tracking variations in the resonance frequency of the cantilever, caused by electrostatic forces between the tip and the sample. 5 It is important to note, that in KPFM measurements the CPD is influenced primarily by the topmost layer of atoms or molecules, making this technique particularly sensitive to surface chemistry and conditions. In the *n*-type semiconductors, band bending occurs upwards due to the depletion of majority carriers in the surface region³⁰³ leading to an upward bending of the local vacuum level and an increase in the work function from the bulk to the surface (Figure 7a). When KPFM is utilized, the local vacuum levels of the sample surface and the tip are equalized. Under light illumination (Figure 7b), photoinduced charge carriers are separated by the built- in electric field in the depletion region, driving holes towards the surface and electrons towards the bulk, resulting in a flattened upward surface band bending. The bulk is grounded, maintaining constant energy levels in the bulk under illumination. The flattened upward band bending reduces the surface work function. Since the work function of the tip remains unchanged under illumination, the SPV of the material can be determined by measuring the CPD under illumination and in the dark. For an n-type semiconductor with upward band bending, as illustrated in Figure 7b, illumination increases the CPD and yields a positive SPV. Conversely, for a p-type semiconductor with downward surface band bending, 303 the separation and transfer of photogenerated electrons towards the surface lead to a decreased CPD and a negative SPV. The measurement of SPV in heterojunction photocatalysts is inherently more complex due to the intricate charge separation processes occurring on multiple surfaces or at interfaces.

One study explored this system from about 0 at. % to 35 at. % Al with near uniform thickness of around 900 nm and demonstrated that thin films can be leveraged to track mechanical property changes over a composition gradient using nanoindentation. 58 Further studies have been performed to understand the interaction effects between the film and substrate for mechanical property determination. As expected, the interaction is dominated by the thickness of the deposited film. However, parameters can be adjusted and thickness-corrections applied to accommodate the substrate interaction zone with previous work showing good agreement between thin film and upscaled materials properties such as the CTE and other mechanical properties. 57, 59-64 Additionally, corrosion behavior can be effectively investigated utilizing the combinatorial thin films rapid material discovery technique. 65 This approach has been applied to a variety of other alloy classes. High entropy alloys (HEAs) or compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) have been investigated using this technique as the optimization and development of these alloys can prove difficult and time-consuming using conventional metallurgical techniques. 66 Other related work with HEA thin films suggests that combinatorial thin films are a promising and cost-effective way to not only investigate properties (such as mechanical properties and corrosion behavior), but are also promising as tools for advanced coating materials. 67-69 Combinatorial synthesis allows for rapid access to vast composition spaces across a variety of material application spaces including electronics, functional materials, and structural materials with the ultimate goal of correlating composition with desired properties. A particular emphasis has been placed on optical and magneto-plasmonic materials. 49-51, 70-76 Other functional materials such as catalytic, 77, 78 magnetic, 79, 80 and electrical⁸¹ materials have also been explored. Structural materials have been explored with a focus on mechanical alloys 57, 59, 65, 82-84 and radiation hard materials. 85, 86 This then shifts the bottleneck from synthesis to characterization of functionality and other material properties. As such, it is then vital to develop a technique to increase throughput while maintaining optimized material functionality.

text: Electrochemical phenomena are the basic operational mechanisms of multiple applications including batteries, fuel cells, memories, and other electrochemical systems. While electrochemical phenomena have been typically explored through macroscopic methods such as electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, ionic motion, or electrochemical reactions, they actually occur at the nanoscale and atomic regimes necessitating high-resolution imaging techniques. This can be achieved using a recently developed atomic force microscopic (AFM) technique, known as electrochemical strain microscopy (ESM). 249, 250 In ESM, when an electric field is applied via the AFM tip, the electric field is concentrated underneath the tip. This triggers ion migration within the material or ionic reactions resulting in a local strain, known as electrochemical strain. When an AC voltage is applied, this mechanical deformation induces oscillations of the tip, which can be detected using a lock-in amplifier that demodulates at the applied AC frequency. By varying the applied voltage and frequency, ESM can provide quantitative information about ionic diffusion coefficients, local ionic conductivity, and electrochemical strain coefficients. 207, 222, 251 The spatial resolution of ESM can typically achieve approximately 20 nm, determined by the size of the AFM tip. However, theoretically, its spatial resolution can be further refined to the order of 3 nm to 10 nm. 252 Indeed, sub-10 nm of the spatial resolution has been reported experimentally. 253 In addition to the typical first harmonic ESM, second harmonic ESM can be used to probe electrochemical dipoles. 254 ESM has been extensively used to explore local electrochemical phenomena. For batteries, this helps to understand phenomena such as lithium intercalation/de-intercalation, phase transformations, and degradation processes. 207, 249, 251, 255-258 For instance, N. Balke et al. visually showed higher ionic mobility at the grain boundaries in a Si anode²⁴⁹ and a different ionic mobility of the solid-electrolyte interphase using ESM. 259 Furthermore, ESM images of Li ion concentration and diffusivity with nanoscale resolution were also shown in LiFePO₄ and LiMn₂O₄. 251, 256 For solid oxide fuel cells (SOFC), as ionic mobility and electrochemical activity at the electrode/electrolyte interface are critical for performance, ESM can provide insights into the ionic transport pathways. 253, 260-262 For instance, in yttrium-stabilized zirconia,
